When ordinary methods fail, the analyst enters into his opponent’s mind and identifies with him. In this way he often sees at once the only means—sometimes absurdly simple ones—of leading the other man into a mistake or rushing him into a wrong calculation.

Whist has long been known to develop what people call the power of calculation. Men of the greatest intelligence have taken what seems an inexplicable pleasure in it, while dismissing chess as trivial. Certainly no similar activity makes such great demands on analytical ability. The best chess player in the Christian world may be little more than a man who plays chess better than anyone else. But excellence at whist suggests an ability to succeed in all those more important activities where one mind competes against another. By excellence I mean complete mastery of the game, including an understanding of every source of fair advantage. These sources are numerous and varied, and often lie in areas of thought quite beyond an ordinary person’s understanding. Close attention produces clear memories; to that extent, the focused chess player will do very well at whist. Hoyle’s rules, based simply on the mechanics of the game, are also clear enough for most people to understand. A good memory and playing by the book are therefore commonly thought to be all that good play requires. But the analyst shows his skill in matters that go beyond any rules. Silently, he makes a great many observations and draws conclusions from them. His companions may do the same. The difference in how much they learn depends less on the soundness of their conclusions than on the quality of their observations. What matters is knowing what to notice. Our player puts no limits on his attention. Although the game is his purpose, he does not dismiss conclusions drawn from things outside it. He studies his partner’s face, carefully comparing it with the faces of both opponents. He considers how each player arranges the cards in his hand, often counting the trumps and high cards one by one from the glances their owners give them. As play continues, he notices every change of expression. Signs of confidence, surprise, triumph, or disappointment give him a wealth of information to consider. The way someone gathers up a trick tells him whether that player can win another in the same suit. The manner in which a card is thrown on the table reveals whether it was played as a bluff. A casual or thoughtless remark; a card accidentally dropped or turned over, and the owner’s anxiety or indifference about keeping it hidden; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are arranged; embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or fear—all give his seemingly instinctive understanding clues to the true state of the game.

When the wedding took place about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service most impressively, and everyone agreed that they had never seen a better-looking bride and groom. But the couple had more than good looks: they were happy. Lord Arthur never regretted for a moment anything he had suffered for Sybil’s sake. She, in return, gave him the finest things a woman could give a man—devotion, tenderness, and love. The realities of life did not destroy their romance. They always felt young.

Some years later, after their two beautiful children were born, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory. This lovely old house had been the Duke’s wedding gift to his son. One afternoon she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime tree in the garden. As they watched the little boy and girl playing along the rose-lined path, darting about like sunbeams, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand. “Are you happy, Sybil?” she asked.

“Dear Lady Windermere, of course I’m happy. Aren’t you?”

“I haven’t time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the latest person I’m introduced to, but generally I grow tired of people as soon as I know them.”

“Don’t your celebrity guests satisfy you, Lady Windermere?”

“Oh dear, no! Those lions are only interesting for one season. Once their manes are cut, they’re the dullest creatures imaginable. Besides, they behave very badly if you’re really nice to them. Do you remember that horrible Mr. Podgers? He was a dreadful fraud. Of course, that didn’t bother me at all, and I even forgave him when he wanted to borrow money. But I couldn’t stand his romantic advances. He’s really made me hate palm reading. I’ve taken up telepathy now. It’s much more entertaining.”

“You mustn’t say anything against palm reading here, Lady Windermere. It’s the only subject Arthur dislikes people joking about. I assure you, he takes it quite seriously.”

“Surely you don’t mean he believes in it, Sybil?”

“Ask him, Lady Windermere. Here he comes.” Lord Arthur walked up the garden carrying a large bunch of yellow roses, with his two children dancing around him.

“Lord Arthur?”

“Yes, Lady Windermere.”

“Surely you don’t mean to say you believe in palm reading?”

“Of course I do,” said the young man with a smile.

“But why?”

“Because I owe all the happiness of my life to it,” he murmured, dropping into a wicker chair.

Shortly after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from a townsman who was away and set off immediately. When they were several miles downstream from Cave Hollow, Tom said:

“Now, you see how this bluff looks the same all the way down from the cave hollow—no houses, no timber yards, just the same bushes everywhere? But see that white patch up there where there’s been a landslide? Well, that’s one of my landmarks. We’ll go ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing you could reach the hole I came out of with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched all around but found nothing. Tom strode proudly into a thick clump of sumac bushes and said:

“Here it is! Look at it, Huck. It’s the coziest hole anywhere around here. Just keep quiet about it. I’ve wanted to be a robber all this time, but I knew I’d need a place like this. Finding one was the problem. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in—because of course there has to be a gang, or it wouldn’t have any style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—that sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“It sure does, Tom. And who will we rob?”

“Oh, just about anybody. Ambush people—that’s mostly how it’s done.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not always. Keep them in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get all they can from their friends, and if they haven’t raised it after you’ve kept them a year, you kill them. That’s the usual way. Except you don’t kill women. You lock the women up, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich and terribly scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take off your hat and speak politely. Nobody’s as polite as robbers—you’ll find that in any book. Well, the women fall in love with you, and after a week or two in the cave they stop crying. After that, you couldn’t make them leave. If you drove them out, they’d turn straight around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, that’s wonderful, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because you’re close to home and circuses and all that.”

By now everything was ready, and the boys went into the hole with Tom leading. They struggled through to the far end of the tunnel, secured their joined kite strings, and continued on.
